description: Hi! We are Synergy, a team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Zacatepec, Mexico. We aim to create software to monitor astronaut health during space missions. We are looking for motivated people interested in data analysis, visualization, AI/ML, UI/UX design, biomedical sciences, and communication. Previous hackathon experience is not required. We value creativity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn!
summary: EIR is an experimental Android health and wellbeing companion designed for astronauts facing isolation, demanding routines, and intermittent communications. It combines a body-centered health dashboard, nutrition and hydration tracking, guided exercise, a four-stage daily checkup, emotional journaling, an on-device AI agent, and step-by-step SOS guidance. Built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, EIR stores records locally and uses an outbox synchronization workflow to exchange data with a Dockerized FastAPI backend deployed on AWS EC2. Camera and voice interactions are exploratory, and example physiological readings are synthetic rather than clinical measurements. By integrating everyday self-awareness, accessible support, and resilient data handling in one interface, EIR demonstrates a practical foundation for future mission-specific, validated astronaut health tools. It does not diagnose medical conditions or replace crew medical officers or authorized emergency procedures.
details:
Health - Body-Centered Health Dashboard

Health provides an overview of preparation status, a selectable human-body representation, contextual information cards, and recent indicators such as heart rate, sleep, hydration, and energy. A body-region selection links the astronaut’s concerns to explanatory text and recent context, helping users navigate health information without searching through unrelated screens. The illustrated measurements and trend lines are demonstration values; they are not automatic medical telemetry or diagnostic outputs.

Habits - Nutrition, Water, and Exercise

Habits brings daily self-care into a single view: consumed and remaining calories, macronutrient progress, water intake against a daily target, scheduled meals, and an exercise routine. The exercise flow includes individual detail screens, sets, repetitions, rest intervals, a running timer, and completion actions. In the spaceflight context these features illustrate how routine adherence could be made visible and manageable. Nutritional targets and workouts shown in the demo are examples, not NASA-approved prescriptions or individualized clinical recommendations.

Checkup - Four-Stage Daily Checkup

checkup guides the user through four sequential steps. First, a facial image is captured through the device camera. Second, a prompted phrase is read into the microphone. Third, the user enters basic indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, and hours slept. Fourth, the user places their perceived emotional state on a two-dimensional mood-and-energy chart and may select a descriptive label. The sequence demonstrates multimodal interaction and structured self-reporting. Camera capture and audio recording must not be represented as validated detection of facial edema, fatigue, respiratory conditions, or other medical conditions; no clinically reliable analysis has been established.

Logbook - Reflection and Continuity

Logbook includes a streak counter, a paced breathing entry point, a two-axis emotional self-assessment, and a daily journal. The journal can be completed with written text or speech-to-text interaction; prior entries are presented in chronological cards with emotional labels and audio affordances. These features support regular reflection and continuity across mission days. Streaks are engagement indicators, not measures of clinical improvement. The mood chart is a subjective self-report rather than a validated mental-health screening instrument.

AI Agent - Local Conversational Assistance

The generic AI Agent module is designed to provide conversational explanations and wellbeing-oriented interaction. The Android source contains an AI ViewModel, a LiteRT-LM engine, and model-download handling for local inference; availability depends on a compatible device and successfully installed model. The prototype also contains demonstration conversation behavior. Accordingly, an example chat screenshot should not be presented as proof that a local model generated the reply unless the model was loaded and that execution was verified. Future development may adapt or fine-tune the assistant for mission-specific knowledge under appropriate funding and evaluation. The agent is not a medical diagnostic system.

SOS - Concise Emergency Guidance

SOS is accessible from a persistent, high-contrast control. The demo presents four emergency categories: dizziness/fainting, chest pain, bleeding or injury, and breathing difficulty. For each scenario, the interface presents short, numbered steps, accompanying illustrations, and an optional audio-reading mode. This is a navigational demonstration, not a certified spacecraft emergency protocol. Any operational adaptation would require review by mission medical and safety authorities, especially where terrestrial first-aid instructions do not transfer directly to microgravity.

Architecture - Android, Local Data, and Backend

The Android application uses Kotlin and Jetpack Compose with ViewModel-managed UI state, repositories, and Retrofit networking. Local persistence is built on SQLite with Room-style entities and DAO interfaces; the repository includes a custom database implementation, so the final technical account should not imply exclusively standard Room code generation. A persistent outbox and WorkManager-based worker support deferred upload. The backend is a Python FastAPI monolith with modular routers for authentication, profiles, health records, wellbeing check-ins, alerts, and synchronization. The team confirms that the same backend code is deployed on AWS EC2. Docker configuration includes Python 3.12, Uvicorn, port 8000, and an eir-data persistent volume for SQLite.

Offline-First Synchronization

When users enter records, the client can retain them locally and queue an outbox operation. When network access is available, the synchronization worker sends pending records to the FastAPI endpoint. The documented workflow distinguishes accepted and duplicate responses (records can be marked synchronized), retryable failures (rescheduled), and rejected/conflict responses (requiring attention). This design aims to reduce loss of user-entered information during communication interruptions. It does not imply that all features work offline: remote authentication and backend-dependent functions still require connectivity, and local model inference requires the model to be installed.

Server Data and Deployment

The backend’s data model separates users, astronaut profiles, sessions, registered devices, health records, wellbeing check-ins, alerts, and synchronization records. Authentication and bootstrap flows are represented in the provided sequence diagram. The deployment diagrams depict both local HTTP testing and a remote HTTPS route using Cloudflare DNS and Caddy reverse proxy. The confirmed fact is deployment of the supplied backend code on EC2; individual infrastructure services and live TLS behavior should be verified against deployment configuration before claiming them as operational.

Risk Alerts - Current Scope

The repository includes an alerts interface and storage-related structures. The supplied risk-engine diagram shows a future pathway from health and wellbeing records through threshold rules to notifications and alert history. Automatic generation of clinically meaningful risk alerts is not established by the available implementation evidence; it is presented as an architectural extension requiring validated thresholds, false-positive assessment, and human oversight.

Scientific Foundation and NASA Relevance

NASA Human Research Program materials on isolation and confinement motivate emotional reflection, sleep awareness, and support access. NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures and Artemis II Standard Measures motivate a cross-domain view of astronaut health rather than isolated metrics. NASA’s Risk of Hypoxia provides context on mission health hazards but does not establish that EIR can detect hypoxia. These sources influenced the design rationale; they are not ingested datasets, and the app does not use private NASA medical records.

Benefits, Impact, and Roadmap

EIR’s principal contribution is the integration of everyday physical-health context, routines, self-reported emotional state, emergency navigation, and an on-device AI pathway into a single, resilient user experience. Potential benefits include reduced interface fragmentation, easier habit tracking, consistent personal records, and accessible guidance. The same interaction model may be relevant to remote field teams and other isolated environments, subject to adaptation. Future work includes validated sensor integrations, mission-specific emergency review, reliable camera/audio analysis, tested local inference, accessibility trials on tablets and external displays, formal privacy/security review, and prospective usability evaluation with relevant experts.

EIR is an experimental prototype. It does not diagnose, triage, or treat medical conditions and does not replace human medical professionals or authorized mission procedures.

Also one of the most important aspects of this experimental prototype is the scalability opportunities it presents, as with proper funding and development it could become a fully fledged project that along with a multidisciplinary could lead to an efficient tool for astronauts to better care for their health, monitor their daily routines and keep a companion that while it doesn't replace human connection it could well serve as an emotional company during long and lonely missions, it's also worthwhile to mention that emotional accompaniment can be integrated to the logbook, making it a more engaging experience than just simply serving as a journaling tool, by integrating AI capabilities also giving this psychological need that sometimes people experiencing isolation and confinement can feel, this of course being optional and never replacing a true health specialist.

Data and Implementation Clarification

The project does not use NASA astronaut personal medical records, proprietary mission data, or NASA physiological datasets directly. NASA and Canadian Space Agency resources were used as scientific and educational references to inform the project rationale, scope, and design.

The physiological indicators included in the demonstration are synthetic, while the wellbeing ratings and journal entries are user-entered demonstration data. These are not NASA data, validated clinical measurements, or operational astronaut monitoring records.

EIR demonstrates software capabilities and possible integration approaches. Further implementation could incorporate authorized NASA resources, validated measurement protocols, and compatible hardware or data sources, subject to availability, permissions, technical integration, and appropriate validation.
